written.myAnswer: Crossing-over exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, creating new combinations of alleles and increasing genetic variation.

In mitotic prophase, chromosomes condense, but homologous chromosomes do not pair and crossing-over does not occur. In prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair, and crossing-over can occur between their non-sister chromatids.
Mitosis preserves the chromosome number in the daughter cells, while meiosis reduces it to half the parent cell’s number.
Sister chromatids are identical copies of a chromosome joined at the centromere. They separate during anaphase II of meiosis.

In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing-over may occur between non-sister chromatids. In metaphase I, homologous pairs align at the equator and attach to spindle fibres. In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles while sister chromatids remain joined. In telophase I, nuclei may reform, and cytokinesis divides the cell into two haploid cells.

Meiosis reduces the chromosome number to form haploid cells, allowing the diploid chromosome number to be restored at fertilization. It also creates genetic variation. In animals it produces gametes; in plants it produces spores.
